reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Site characterization is essential for safe and economical driven pile design. In-situ testing is integral to the program. Quality and completeness of geotechnical information directly affects all subsequent design and construction decisions.
sections.body: A site characterization program is a necessary component for the safe and economical design of a driven pile foundation. In-situ testing of soil and rock is integral to a site characterization program and is further discussed in Chapter 5. The quality and reliability of the geotechnical information obtained during the site characterization directly affects the foundation design and construction process.
key_points: Site characterization is essential for safe and economical driven pile foundation design
In-situ testing of soil and rock is integral to the program
Quality of geotechnical information directly affects design and construction outcomes
sections.applicability: Overview of the site characterization program for driven pile foundation projects.

sections.title: Site Characterization Program
sections.summary: Three exploration phases: (1) office data collection, (2) field reconnaissance, and (3) detailed subsurface exploration (borings, sampling, in-situ testing). Each phase builds on the previous. Single-phase programs common for small projects; staged programs for large or design-build projects.
sections.body: Site characterization encompasses gathering and reporting site conditions required to safely and economically design foundations. The information needed varies depending on site geologic conditions, foundation types, structural performance requirements, acceptable risk, and constructability. The site exploration consists of three main phases: (1) planning the exploration program and data collection (office work), (2) field reconnaissance survey, and (3) detailed subsurface exploration (boring, sampling, and in-situ testing). Table 4-1 lists the purpose of each phase.
key_points: Three exploration phases: office planning, field reconnaissance, detailed subsurface exploration
Each phase adds to or supplements the previous phase
Single-phase programs common for small projects; staged programs for large or design-build projects
Information must address geologic conditions, foundation types, performance requirements, and constructability
sections.applicability: Framework for organizing and executing a subsurface exploration program for driven pile projects.

sections.title: Data Collection
sections.summary: Office phase: gather structural information from bridge design office plus general subsurface data from geotechnical databases, topographic maps (USGS), agricultural soil surveys (USDA), aerial photos, well records, and geologic maps (Table 4-2). Prepares engineer for field reconnaissance and identifies problem areas.
sections.body: The data collection phase obtains information about the proposed structure and general subsurface conditions. Structural information comes from the bridge design office and preliminary structure plans. General subsurface information is obtained from a variety of sources listed in Table 4-2, including geotechnical databases, construction records, topographic maps (USGS), county agricultural soil survey maps (USDA), aerial photos or satellite imagery, well drilling records, and geologic maps. This phase prepares the engineer for the field reconnaissance survey and identifies possible problems and areas to scrutinize.
key_points: Obtain structural information from bridge design office and preliminary structure plans
Sources of subsurface information include geotechnical databases, construction records, topographic maps, aerial photos, well drilling records, and geologic maps
Data collection prepares the engineer for field reconnaissance
Identifies possible problems and areas requiring additional scrutiny
Additional sources of historical data are listed in GEC-5, Sabatini et al. (2002)
sections.applicability: Office-based data collection phase of site characterization for driven pile foundation design.

sections.title: Field Reconnaissance Survey
sections.summary: Site visit to identify constructability issues (access, headroom, utilities), inspect nearby structures for foundation performance, check stream banks for scour, and examine terrain for landslides. Findings guide boring program planning. Example reconnaissance form per AASHTO Foundation Investigation Manual (1978).
sections.body: Site visits by the geotechnical engineer and other design team members are necessary to properly characterize the site. Field reconnaissance presents an opportunity to locate and record constructability issues such as site access, headroom restrictions, and other working conditions that may be overlooked from reviewing site or aerial photos. The field reconnaissance includes inspection of nearby structures, inspection of existing footings and stream banks for scour, recording of existing structures, visual examination for evidence of landslides, location of trees and surface water, and relating site conditions to proposed boring operations. Figure 4-1 contains an example of a field reconnaissance form modified from the AASHTO Foundation Investigation Manual (1978).
key_points: Site visits are necessary to verify and supplement office phase information
Locate and record constructability issues: site access, headroom, utilities
Inspect nearby structures for foundation performance
Check existing footings and stream banks for evidence of scour and movement
Examine terrain for evidence of landslides
Record features and constraints that impact constructability of potential foundation systems
Geotechnical loading requirements dictate field exploration program planning
sections.applicability: Field reconnaissance phase of site characterization for driven pile foundations.

sections.title: Detailed Field Exploration
sections.summary: Detailed borings, sampling, and in-situ testing form the factual basis for pile design. Major structures use a two-phase approach: pilot borings during planning for preliminary profile, then control borings at key locations and verification borings to fill gaps. Geophysical surveys and in-situ testing supplement conventional borings.
sections.body: The purpose of the field exploration program is to obtain representative information on subsurface conditions, to recover disturbed and undisturbed soil samples, to perform in-situ testing, and to determine groundwater levels. This information provides the factual basis for all subsequent steps in pile design and construction. The field exploration plan focuses on items related to the design of driven pile foundations. For major structures, pilot borings are performed at select locations during preliminary planning to establish a preliminary subsurface profile, followed by a two-phase boring program: control borings at key locations, then verification borings to fill in gaps.
key_points: Provides factual basis for all subsequent pile design and construction steps
Quality and completeness of subsurface data are paramount
First step is a preliminary boring, sampling, and in-situ testing plan
For major structures: pilot borings during planning, then control + verification borings
Geophysical surveys and in-situ testing supplement conventional borings
Preliminary structural design plan should be established to ensure borings are properly located
sections.applicability: Detailed subsurface exploration planning for driven pile foundation design.

sections.title: Geophysical Surveys
sections.summary: Geophysical surveys supplement borings over large areas. Methods: seismic surface wave (bedrock depth, Vs, groundwater), ground penetrating radar (near-surface voids to 6–9 m, not effective in saturated clay), and electrical resistivity (soil strata changes, voids, buried objects). Always combine with direct exploration.
sections.body: Geophysical surveys aid in subsurface characterization over a wide area and supplement borings and other invasive tests. Primarily, seismic and electrical methods are used to measure depth to groundwater and bedrock and to resolve intermediate soil strata thickness. These methods may identify and locate subsurface anomalies requiring further evaluation by soil borings or in-situ tests. Geophysical surveys may also locate voids, debris, or buried objects as well as measure divisions in soil stiffness. Seismic surface wave methods use impact or ambient noise to produce surface waves analyzed for soil stiffness, bedrock depth, and groundwater depth. Ground penetrating radar detects near-surface voids in the 20-30 foot depth range but is not effective in saturated clayey soils. Electrical resistivity measures soil strata changes and locates voids or buried objects.
key_points: Supplement borings and other invasive tests over a wide area
Seismic and electrical methods measure depth to groundwater, bedrock, and soil strata thickness
Can locate voids, debris, buried objects, and subsurface anomalies
Seismic surface wave methods analyze soil stiffness from reflected waves
Ground penetrating radar useful for near-surface voids (20-30 ft) but not in saturated clays
Electrical resistivity can distinguish coarse vs fine-grained materials and locate groundwater
Should always be performed in combination with direct exploration methods (borings, in-situ tests)
sections.applicability: Non-invasive subsurface characterization to supplement boring and in-situ testing programs.

sections.title: Depth, Spacing, and Frequency of Boring and In-Situ Tests
sections.summary: Minimum exploration points: 1 per substructure (width ≤ 30 m) or 2 per substructure (width > 30 m) (Table 4-3). Minimum depth: 6 m below expected pile toe or 2× pile group width, whichever governs. For piles on rock: minimum 3 m of rock coring. Borings must extend through weak strata (peat, organics, soft clay) to competent support material.
sections.body: The cost of a subsurface exploration program is small relative to the foundation cost; however, in the absence of adequate boring data, the engineer must rely on conservative designs with high safety margins. The number of borings, their spacing, and sampling intervals depend on the uniformity of soil strata and loading conditions. Table 4-3 provides minimum quantity guidelines for exploration points per substructure. Minimum exploration depths should extend 20 feet below expected pile toe elevation, or at least two times the pile group width. For piles on rock, at least 10 feet of rock coring should be performed. In-situ test spacing and frequency should be determined based on project requirements, supplementing borings where undisturbed sampling is not easily performed.
key_points: Cost of exploration is small compared to foundation cost
Erratic subsurface conditions require closely spaced borings
W <= 100 ft: minimum 1 exploration point per substructure; W > 100 ft: minimum 2 points
Minimum depth: 20 ft below expected pile toe or 2x pile group width
For piles on rock: at least 10 ft of rock coring
Additional boring and in-situ testing depths may be required due to site-specific geology
Borings should extend through unsuitable soil strata (peat, organic material, soft fine-grained soils) to reach suitable foundation support materials
Liquefaction and aggressive environment studies may dictate appropriate sampling intervals
sections.applicability: Guidelines for boring layout and depth for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Soil Boring Methods
sections.summary: Common methods (Table 4-4): auger borings (hollow stem acts as casing, most common, to 60 m), rotary drilling (4–6 inch diameter to 60+ m), wash borings (light equipment, limited to fine materials), and sonic coring (up to 300 m, near-100% recovery, collects any soil type). Drilling mud can contaminate recovered samples.
sections.body: Soil borings are the most frequently used exploration technique and offer the ability to collect disturbed and undisturbed samples and to perform in-situ tests. Common methods include augered borings, wash borings, rotary drilling, and sonic drilling, summarized in Table 4-4. Continuous flight augers (solid or hollow stem) bore into the subsurface for sampling and testing; hollow stem augers act as casing and range from 2.25 to 12.25 inch I.D. Rotary drilling uses a drill bit to cut and grind material, with water or drilling mud flushing cuttings. Wash borings are advanced by chopping action of a light bit with water jetting. Sonic coring can collect any soil type with minimal fluids up to 1000 feet.
key_points: Auger borings: most common, can drill to 100-200 ft; hollow stem acts as casing
Rotary drilling: suited for 4-6 inch diameter borings to 200+ ft; rapid method in most soils and rock
Wash borings: light equipment, inexpensive, but slow and not suited for stones/boulders
Sonic coring: up to 1000 ft, generally 100% recovery, collects soils and bedrock with minimal fluids
Drilling mud can contaminate recovered soil samples
Wash borings infrequently used in the United States
sections.applicability: Selection of soil boring methods for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Soil Sampling Methods
sections.summary: Disturbed samples: split barrel (SPT, ASTM D1586; 35 mm ID, 51 mm OD), sonic cores, or test pits. Undisturbed samples: thin-walled Shelby tubes (ASTM D1587, for fine-grained soils), piston samplers (prevent premature entry), or Pitcher sampler (alternating hard/soft layers). No sample is completely undisturbed.
sections.body: Soil samples may be collected via disturbed or undisturbed methods. Disturbed samples are collected with a split barrel sampler, sonic cores, or test pits and are used for visual classification and routine laboratory testing. The standard split spoon sampler for SPT has an inner diameter of 1.375 inches and outer diameter of 2 inches (ASTM D1586), shown in Figure 4-2. Relatively undisturbed samples are collected with thin walled tubes (Shelby tubes, Figure 4-3), piston samplers, or the Pitcher sampler. Thin walled tubes are typically used for fine-grained soils; piston samplers prevent soil from entering the tube prematurely; the Pitcher sampler can sample alternating hard and soft layers. ASTM D1587 provides detailed guidance on thin walled tube sampling.
key_points: Disturbed samples: split barrel sampler (SPT), sonic cores, or test pits
Standard SPT sampler: 1.375 in ID, 2 in OD (ASTM D1586)
Undisturbed samples: thin walled tubes (Shelby tubes, ASTM D1587), piston samplers, Pitcher sampler
No sample will be completely undisturbed even with utmost care
Thin walled tubes are typically used for fine-grained soils
Piston samplers prevent soil from entering tube before sampling
Pitcher sampler is attractive for alternating hard and soft layers
sections.applicability: Soil sampling equipment and techniques for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Rock Exploration Methods (Coring / Drilling)
sections.summary: Wire line rotary coring preferred for depths > 24 m; conventional rotary for shallow rock. Rock Quality Designation (RQD, ASTM D6032) = sum of sound core pieces ≥ 100 mm / total run length: Excellent 90–100%, Good 75–90%, Fair 50–75%, Poor 25–50%, Very Poor < 25%. Cores retained in boxes with notation of bedding, fractures, and weathering.
sections.body: Rock drilling and coring is typically performed at the end of a soil boring once bedrock is encountered. Special drilling bits cut and grind through rock while fluid or air flushes out cuttings. The recovered rock core is classified by rock type, recovery length, and recovery percentage. Table 4-5 summarizes rock coring methods: conventional rotary coring, wire line rotary coring (preferred for depths > 80 ft), and rotary coring of swelling clay or soft rock. Rock cores should be stored in structurally sound core boxes (Figure 4-4) with careful notation of bedding, fractures, and weathered zones. Rock cores are given a Rock Quality Designation (RQD) per ASTM D6032, defined as the sum of sound core pieces >= 4 inches in length divided by the total core run length, expressed as a percentage. Table 4-6 provides RQD designations: Excellent (90-100), Good (75-90), Fair (50-75), Poor (25-50), Very Poor (<25).
key_points: Rock coring performed after soil boring encounters bedrock
Conventional rotary, wire line rotary, and swelling clay/soft rock coring methods available
Wire line rotary coring preferred for depths > 80 ft due to faster retrieval
Rock cores stored in core boxes with notation of bedding, fractures, and weathering
RQD (ASTM D6032) = sum of sound core pieces >= 4 in / total core run length
RQD designations: Excellent (90-100), Good (75-90), Fair (50-75), Poor (25-50), Very Poor (<25)
Core samples should be retained for project duration and beyond for construction claims
RQD alone should not be used to correlate rock strength
sections.applicability: Rock exploration and quality assessment for driven pile foundations bearing on or driven to rock.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.summary: Monitor water levels during drilling, at boring completion, and 24 hours after; low-permeability cohesive soils may require > 1 week for equilibrium. Observation wells (slotted PVC) monitor unconfined water table; piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire) monitor confined aquifer hydrostatic pressure. Essential for effective stress analysis and construction dewatering planning.
sections.body: Accurate groundwater level information is needed for estimating soil densities, determining effective soil pressures, preparing effective stress diagrams, and indicating construction difficulties that may be encountered. Water levels should be monitored during drilling, upon completion of boring, and 24 hours after completion. More than one week may be required for representative readings in low-permeability cohesive soils or bore holes stabilized with drilling muds. Observation wells (slotted PVC pipe) monitor water level changes in a select aquifer, while piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire diaphragm devices) monitor hydrostatic pressure changes in a confined aquifer or specific stratum. Additional piezometer information is available in FHWA-NHI-01-031 (Mayne et al. 2002).
key_points: Groundwater levels needed for soil density estimation, effective stress calculations, and construction planning
Monitor water levels during drilling, at boring completion, and 24 hours after
Low permeability soils may require > 1 week for representative water level readings
Observation wells (slotted PVC pipe) for unconfined water table monitoring
Piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire) for confined aquifer hydrostatic pressure monitoring
Single and multiple piezometers can be installed in a single bore hole
sections.applicability: Groundwater characterization for effective stress analysis and construction planning in driven pile projects.

sections.title: Information Required for Construction
sections.summary: Site characterization data drives: pile type selection, hammer sizing, installation aid determination (predrilling, jetting), cost estimation, bid documents, construction control methods, and schedules. Pile type from local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions; size and length from soil properties and bearing layers. Well-defined characterization reduces unplanned cost and contractor claims.
sections.body: The subsurface exploration and subsequent soil and rock testing program provides essential information for driven pile design and construction. Engineers and contractors use this information to select pile type, size hammer equipment, determine if installation aids are needed, prepare cost estimates and bid documents, establish construction control methods, and generate construction schedules. Pile type is generally selected based on local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions, while size and length depend on soil properties and bearing layers. Pile drivability and other construction considerations are affected by the overall site characterization including permeability, relative density, layering, and soil response to pile driving.
key_points: Subsurface data essential for pile type selection, hammer sizing, and installation aid determination
Used to prepare cost estimates, bid documents, and construction schedules
Pile type selected based on local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions
Pile size and length depend on soil properties and bearing layers
Drivability affected by permeability, relative density, layering, and soil response to driving
Well-defined site characterization reduces risk of unplanned cost and claims
sections.applicability: Use of site characterization data for driven pile construction planning and cost estimation.
